text: Now that orders.csv is clean, it's time to build new columns on top of it — some with simple math, some with logic that needs a real function. This is where a DataFrame starts doing actual work for you.

quantity times unit_price, applied to the whole column in one line — no loop, no apply needed. That's called a vectorized operation: pandas, through NumPy underneath, multiplies every row at once. Whenever the logic is simple arithmetic like this, vectorized beats apply every time.

But apply earns its place the moment the logic isn't pure arithmetic. Here, a lambda labels each order Large if its total clears two hundred dollars, Standard otherwise — that's a conditional, one function call per value, and six orders end up Large.

Remember order 1014's negative quantity? clip with lower equals zero clamps any value below zero up to zero, giving you a usable number instead of a missing row. But notice it doesn't retroactively fix line_total, which was already computed from the original negative quantity — order of operations matters in a real pipeline.

The dot-str accessor exposes ordinary string methods — upper, strip, contains — across an entire column at once. df of region dot str dot upper is the vectorized equivalent of calling upper on every value in a loop.

You can now derive new columns with both math and custom logic. Next lesson zooms out from individual rows entirely: groupby and aggregation, to summarize this whole dataset by category and by region.
